content: The role of neoadjuvant chemotherapy in the management of locally advanced cervical cancer remains uncertain, and its impact varies depending on specific treatment protocols. This review analyzed individual patient data to evaluate the effects of neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by either radical radiotherapy or surgery, compared to radical radiotherapy alone. To gather data, comprehensive searches were conducted in Medline, CancerLit, and trial registries, supplemented by manual searches of conference proceedings and direct communication with trial investigators. The search was updated as of February 2006. Only randomized trials involving patients with locally advanced cervical cancer who received neoadjuvant chemotherapy prior to radiotherapy or surgery were included. Data from these trials were collected, validated, and re-analyzed. Queries were resolved by the trial investigators, and the final data were verified. Treatment comparisons were analyzed separately, and hazard ratios were calculated using a fixed-effect model. Pre-specified subgroup analyses were performed to assess whether trial design or patient/tumor characteristics influenced the outcomes of neoadjuvant chemotherapy. For the first comparison, data from 18 trials involving 2,074 patients were analyzed. A high degree of statistical heterogeneity was observed, much of which was explained by differences in trial design. Trials that used chemotherapy cycle lengths shorter than 14 days (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.83, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.69 to 1.00, p = 0.046) or cisplatin dose intensities greater than 25 mg/m² per week (HR = 0.91, 95% CI = 0.78 to 1.05, p = 0.20) tended to show a survival benefit with neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Conversely, trials with cycle lengths longer than 14 days (HR = 1.25, 95% CI = 1.07 to 1.46, p = 0.005) or cisplatin dose intensities below 25 mg/m² per week (HR = 1.35, 95% CI = 1.11 to 1.64, p = 0.002) demonstrated a detrimental effect on survival. For the second comparison, data from 5 trials involving 872 patients were analyzed. The combined results (HR = 0.65, 95% CI = 0.53 to 0.80, p = 0.0004) showed a significant reduction in the risk of death with neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgery compared to radical radiotherapy alone. However, there was heterogeneity in both trial design and results. The findings suggest that the timing and dose intensity of cisplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy are critical factors influencing its effectiveness in women with locally advanced cervical cancer. These factors warrant further investigation. Additionally, obtaining more individual patient data may strengthen the reliability of these conclusions.
